title: Address at Ellensburg, Washington
paragraphs: Mr. Mayor; and My Fellow Citizens; My Fellow Americans:

It is the greatest pleasure to be with you to-day. First of all let me greet those whom I know the others will not grudge my specially greeting -- the men of the Grand Army and the representatives of those who did even more than the men of the civil war, the women; (Cheers and applause) for while the men went to battle, to the woman fell the harder task of seeing husband or lover, father or brother, going to the war, and she herself having [?] to stay behind with the load of doubt, anxiety and uncertainty and often the hard difficulty of making both ends meet in the household while the breadwinner was away.

In a state like Washington with its record of active and vigorous life, with in it representatives of the men who fought as the men of the old war fought I do not wonder that her sons did so well in the Philippines and I am not surprised that you here should have sent a company which as I understand it lost more than almost any other company of all the troops in the Philippines. They were my brethren, my comrades in our war, which was a very little war compared to yours, but still we had a job to do and we did it. (Applause)

Let me say a special word of greeting to those at the other end -- the children. I have greeted the veterans, now I want to greet the children specially. I am very, very glad to see you. I have got just one word to say to you and it applies almost as well to your elders. I believe in play and I believe in work. Play hard while you play, and when you work do not play at all. (Applause) In congratulating you of Washington upon your lumber, your commerce, upon your great coal fields, upon the cattle on a thousand hills, in congratulating you upon all your products I congratulate you most upon the children. They seem all right in quality and in quantity, and as I believe in your stock I am glad it is being kept up. (Applause) It has pleased me particularly coming through this mighty state with its extraordinary capacity for industrial development to see that you, the men and women who are developing it, at the same time that you are taking the fullest advantage of your material resources are taking care to build upon those as a foundation the higher life, that you are taking thought for the next generation, taking thought for the country, for the people that are to come after you. No men do their duty or pretend to do their duty if they simply think of their own interests, if they do not shape the governmental policy, their social policy, for the country as a whole, the country that is to come after them. Exactly as every man worth his salt, or woman worth her salt, will care even more for the future of their children than for their own well-being, so in this nation we are bound in honor to shape our present policy with a view to the nation's future needs; to do as you did in the civil war, You went to war, you faced four years of conflict, that the generations that came after you for the centuries to come should live in union and in peace within our borders. (Applause) So when you provide for the training and upbuilding of the children, when you provide for the schools -- the high school, the normal school, the academy, the college -- you are building firm and wide and deep the foundation for the might and greatness of the future; for after all, important though the material resources are, important though your wheat, your lumber, your fisheries, your cattle, your mines, your commerce, your factories are, most important of all is the standard of good citizenship which you produce. I congratulate Washington upon its school system, upon all its schools from the simplest to the highest; and I say a word of special greeting to those engaged in teaching, to the teachers, the educators. No other body of men or women in time of peace does a more important work than those upon whose teaching and example and sympathy and self-abnegation and enthusiasm so much depends for the future generation. Yet the men and women must remember that you cannot put off upon the teachers the whole duty of educating the next generation. Fathers and mothers must educate the children in their own homes by precept and by example, and just let me say this, that if your precepts and your examples differ you cannot expect good results for the children. There is no use in preaching truth where mendacity is sometimes practiced. There is no use preaching unselfishness if the father consistently leads a selfish life. There is no use preaching the gospel of work if the father and mother shirk work. There is no use preaching the gospel of duty if there is no attempt to perform duty on the part of those who preach it. A father and mother have a duty in educating their children of which no one can relieve them. The teachers can do much, but after all it is the help in the home which can do most. (Applause)

I also want to say a word upon the kinds of quality which we need in citizenship, for we [?] need more than one kind. In the first place you need decency, honesty, the spirit of fair dealing, the spirit that makes a man a good neighbor, a good friend, the spirit that makes a man do his duty by the state. If you have not the foundation of clean living and fair dealing in you then the greater a man's ability is the worse he is for the whole community. It is just as it was in the civil war; if the man had not the spirit of loyalty, of obedience, of faith to the flag, of faith to the nation, then the stronger, the abler, the more cunning he was, the more dangerous he was. In his regiment he was a cause of disturbance; outside the regiment he would come very near being a traitor to the nation. So in civic life, exactly as bodily strength if unaccompanied by any spirit of self-restraint makes a man a dange rous brute, while at the same if guided aright it makes him a most valuable citizen, so mere intellectual ability, the power that makes a man able to rise in the world, his smartness, his business capacity, his shrewdness, if there is not a backing of moral sense behind it, makes him the more dangerous. In this country we urgently need to have it established that the weight of public opinion shall be felt just as heavily against the scoundrel who succeeds as against the scoundrel who fails. (Applause) But that is not enough. Exactly as in the civil war you needed patriotism first, but the patriotism did not count if the man ran away, so it is in civil life. In additi on to the spirit of decency, of fair dealing, of honesty, you must have the strong, virile virtues, the virtues that make a man able to hold his own in the world, to make his weight felt as of moment in the larger life.of the nation. It is not enough to mean well when you sit at home. You have got to be able to do well when you get out into the actual field where civic life is waged; you have got to be able to do well in your trade, in business, to keep your family, to make yourself felt, to bring up your children so that they shall go upward a little, to make yourself count whatever your part. The virtue that sits at home in its own parlor and bemoans how bad the world is never yet benefitted anyone. What we need is the type of decent man who can go out and hold his own against all comers, who without losing his sense of decency can make himself felt as a man of weight wherever he is put. That applies in the education of children. Let me come back to that for just one moment. One thing that always makes me feel a little melancholy is to see fathers and mothers who themselves have worked hard and led useful lives but who in a queer misguided spirit of foolish affection, try to save their children from trouble by also saving them from being of any earthly use in the world. That is not affection; that is folly; And I do not care at which end of the social line it is. You all know among your own neighbors a man, and I am sorry to say sometimes a woman, who will say "Well, I have worked hard, my boys shall enjoy themselves"; or if the woman, she will say "I have had to work hard and my girls shall be ladies;" under the foolish belief that to be a lady means that you are not to work, not to do, not to be of any use in the world. Those parents are preparing for their children a life of misery, and a life of uselessness; because of all forms of life that which on the whole is the least attractive, which has the least real joy in it, is the life consciously developed of nothing but the pursuit of pleasure; [?] It is but the meanest type of life that there is to lead. In '61 there were lots of people in the co untry who were too fond of ease to go into war, and the easy thing to do was to stay at home and say the country could not be saved; the hard thing was to go out and save it. Those men stayed at home, they walked delicately, they lived in the earth's soft places, while you had what you could carry on your backs and lay where night overtook you and marched until you were so footsore and weary that you thought you could not keep up any longer. You found the blanket so heavy that if you were a recruit you threw it away and at midnight wished you had two. You did that for four years while the others lived at ease. And which had the real life, which had the life that was worth living, which is proud now to hand on the heritage of what was done, the man that did nothing? The man that risked, and fought, and labored, and shed his blood, he is the man who co unts, he is the man who had a good time in life. I do not pity any man because he has to work at something worth doing and does it well. I admire him. So it is in civil life. Train your children not how to avoid difficulties but how to overcome them; train your children not to shirk what is hard and disagreeable but to do it and to do it well. I believe in this country; I believe in you and those like you because I know that in this country the average citizen has in him or in her the power to lead just that kind of life, has within his soul the spirit that drives him on to work for worthy ends, and to win triumph as the result.
My fellow citizens, I have enjoyed to the full coming here to greet you this morning -- the men, the women and the children. It has done me good to see you. (Cheers and applause)
